title: Measuring Weight in Grade 2: Grams and Kilograms Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: Measuring Weight Grade 2: Grams & Kilograms + Quiz
meta_desc: A simple Grade 2 guide to measuring weight in grams and kilograms: balance vs scale, estimate then check, plus a free 8-question quiz to practise.
excerpt: A biscuit is weighed in grams, a bag of atta in kilograms — and a seven-year-old needs to feel the difference before the numbers make sense. Here is how I teach measuring weight in Grade 2, with a quick quiz to check what has stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a seven-year-old a single biscuit and a full bag of atta and ask which is heavier. Easy — the atta, obviously. Now ask how much heavier, and the guessing starts. That gap is exactly what measuring weight in Grade 2 is about: moving a child from ‘this one feels heavier’ to putting a real number on it using grams and kilograms. In this guide I’ll walk through how I teach standard units of weight to Grade 2 — the balance, the weighing scale, and the everyday feel for what a gram and a kilogram actually are.

One boundary first. In Grade 2 we are only asking how heavy something is. Not how long it is, not how much a jug can hold. Keep weight in its own box in the child’s head; length and capacity are different lessons for a different day.

Grams and kilograms: the two units Grade 2 needs

At this age a child needs exactly two standard units of weight and nothing more: the gram (g) for light things and the kilogram (kg) for heavy things. That is the whole toolkit. A biscuit, a pencil, a coin — grams. A school bag, a watermelon, a bag of rice — kilograms.

The mistake I see is jumping straight to conversions before a child has any feel for the units. Do not. First let them hold a 1 kg pack of sugar in one hand and a single biscuit in the other, over and over, until the words ‘gram’ and ‘kilogram’ carry a physical memory. The maths sits on top of that feeling.

A feel for 1 kg = 1000 g

Here is the one number fact for the year: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. That is a big number for a seven-year-old, so anchor it to something real. A standard pack of sugar or atta from the kirana shop is 1 kg. Tell them that same pack could be written as 1000 g — same weight, different unit, like saying ‘one rupee’ or ‘hundred paise’.

I would not push hard on converting numbers yet. If a child can tell you that 1 kg and 1000 g are the same, and that 2 kg is 2000 g, that is plenty for Grade 2. The deeper conversion practice belongs to Grade 3 and 4.

The balance, or taraazu: comparing two things

Before any scale gives a number, children should meet the balance — the taraazu with two pans. It answers one question beautifully: which of two things is heavier? Put an apple in one pan and an eraser in the other. The pan that dips down holds the heavier thing; the pan that rises holds the lighter one. If the pans sit level, the two weigh the same.

This is where heavier and lighter stop being vague words and become something a child can see. You can build a rough balance at home with a coat hanger and two paper cups, and it works well enough to make the point.

The weighing scale: putting a number on it

The balance compares. The weighing scale — the kitchen scale or the flat digital one — measures. It gives an actual number in grams or kilograms. This is the step from ‘the apple is heavier’ to ‘the apple is 150 g’.

Let the child place an object on the scale and read the number aloud. Weigh five or six things from around the house and write each one down. Seeing that a spoon reads 30 g while a textbook reads 1 kg does more for their sense of the units than any worksheet can.

Estimate first, then check

This is my favourite routine, and the one that builds real number sense. Before anything goes on the scale, the child guesses the weight. Then they weigh it and see how close they were. Being wrong is the whole point — each wrong guess quietly corrects their internal ruler.

  • Pick an everyday object — a mango, a shoe, a water bottle.
  • Ask: grams or kilograms? Light things go in grams, heavy things in kilograms.
  • Write down a guess, out loud, before weighing.
  • Weigh it on the scale and read the real number.
  • Talk about the gap: closer next time?

After a week of this, most children stop making wild guesses like ‘a mango weighs 5 kg’ and settle into sensible ranges. That settling is exactly the skill Grade 2 is training.

Grams or kilograms? A quick sorting table

The single most useful judgement at this level is picking the right unit before you even weigh. Light enough to hold easily in one hand? Probably grams. Heavy enough that you notice lifting it? Probably kilograms. Here is a table I use to drill that choice.

ObjectBest unitRoughly
One biscuitGrams (g)about 10 g
An appleGrams (g)about 150 g
A full water bottleGrams (g)about 500 g
A bag of attaKilograms (kg)1 kg or more
A school bag with booksKilograms (kg)about 3 kg
A watermelonKilograms (kg)about 4 kg

One honest caveat: these numbers are approximate and will vary. The goal is not for a child to memorise that an apple is 150 g — it is to know that an apple belongs in grams and a watermelon in kilograms. Get the unit right and the number can be checked on the scale.

Try the quiz, then the printable worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly what we covered — grams versus kilograms, reading a balance, and 1 kg = 1000 g. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Grade 2 Measuring Weight Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on grams and kilograms, the balance, and estimating weight. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 measuring weight in grams and kilograms

questions.q: Which is the best unit to weigh a bag of atta (flour)?
questions.explanation: A bag of atta is heavy, so we weigh it in kilograms (kg). Grams are for light things.

questions.q: How many grams are equal to 1 kilogram?
questions.explanation: 1 kilogram = 1000 grams. A 1 kg pack of sugar is the same as 1000 g.
A brick is by far the heaviest. A feather, a paper clip and a biscuit are all very light.

questions.q: You want to weigh one small biscuit. Which unit is best?
questions.explanation: A biscuit is very light, so we use grams (g). Metres measure length and hours measure time.

questions.q: On a balance (taraazu), which pan goes DOWN?
options: The pan with the lighter thing
The pan with the heavier thing
questions.explanation: The heavier thing pulls its pan down. The lighter pan rises up.

questions.q: Which of these would you weigh in kilograms, not grams?
options: A school bag full of books
questions.explanation: A full school bag is heavy, so kilograms fit best. The others are light and belong in grams.

questions.q: 2 kilograms is the same as how many grams?
questions.explanation: 1 kg is 1000 g, so 2 kg is 2000 g. Just double the 1000.

questions.q: A bunch of bananas weighs 500 g. That is the same as...
questions.explanation: 1000 g makes 1 kg, so 500 g is half of that — half a kilogram.

faq.q: What weight units should a Grade 2 child know?
faq.a: Just two standard units: the gram (g) for light things like a biscuit or a pencil, and the kilogram (kg) for heavy things like a bag of atta or a school bag. That, plus knowing 1 kg = 1000 g, is the whole Grade 2 target.

faq.q: What is the difference between a balance and a weighing scale?
faq.a: A balance (taraazu) compares two things and tells you which is heavier — the pan that dips down holds the heavier object. A weighing scale gives an actual number, like 150 g or 2 kg. Children should meet the balance first, then the scale.

faq.q: Does my child need to do gram-to-kilogram conversions in Grade 2?
faq.a: Only very simple ones. If they know 1 kg is 1000 g and can see that 2 kg is 2000 g, that is enough. Full conversion practice with tricky numbers belongs to Grade 3 and 4.

faq.q: How do I build a real feel for weight at home?
faq.a: Use the estimate-then-check routine. Before weighing an object, have your child guess in grams or kilograms, then put it on the scale and compare. A week of guessing everyday items fixes wild estimates fast.
